description.value: The study evaluated the effect of 24-hour smoking abstinence on brain responses to smoking-related visual cues in adult smokers using fMRI.

spans.text: The current investigation sought to evaluate the effects of 24-hr tobacco abstinence on brain responses to visual smoking cues in dependent smokers.

value: 24-hr smoking abstinence would increase brain activation in response to smoking cues in regions subserving reward, motivation and affective processes.

spans.text: We hypothesized that, consistent with incentive motivation models of drug use, 24-hr smoking abstinence would increase brain activation in response to smoking cues in regions subserving reward, motivation and affective processes.

description.value: Within-subject repeated-measures study with two counterbalanced fMRI sessions: one following usual smoking and one following 24-hour abstinence.

spans.text: Following the training period, participants completed two fMRI sessions that were identical except that prior to one session they were allowed to smoke their usual amount of cigarettes up until entering the scanning facility (satiated condition) while in the other session they were required to be 24-hrs abstinent from smoking prior to, and following, scanning (abstinent condition).
Order of condition was randomly assigned and counterbalanced.

value: Following 24-hr abstinence, greater activation was found in response to smoking cues compared to control cues in parietal regions, posterior cingulate, dorsal striatum, frontal and occipital cortex, central cortical regions, cerebellum, and dorsal thalamus.

These findings suggest that following smoking abstinence, smoking cues robustly activate corticostriatal areas possibly involved in processing smoking-related sensory information and planning or selecting relevant actions.

spans.text: Following 24-hr abstinence, greater activation was found in response to smoking cues compared to control cues in parietal regions including right superior parietal lobule and bilateral precuneus (BA 7); bilateral posterior cingulate (BA 31); striatum including bilateral putamen and internal capsule; left superior frontal gyrus (BA 8/9); left occipital cortex (BA 19); right dorsal thalamus; bilateral cerebellum; and central cortical regions including right pre/postcentral gyrus and bilateral paracentral lobule (BA 4).

value: When activation was contrasted between the two conditions, 24-hr abstinence resulted in greater activation than satiety in left superior frontal gyrus, right superior parietal lobule, right posterior cingulate gyrus, bilateral occipital cortex, a region on the boundary between right pre- and post-central gyrus, and right caudate/internal capsule.

The present findings suggest that smoking abstinence potentiates neural responding to smoking-related cues, possibly reflecting an increase in the incentive salience of these cues resulting from increased smoking motivation.
